evidence_set: PATH Wave 1 (2013–2014): 247 adults who only vaped against 2,411 who only smoked cigarettes (220 against 2,322 for the volatile-compound markers), geometric means per mg creatinine, adjusted for creatinine, age, sex, race/ethnicity, education, marijuana use in the past 30 days and weekly hours of second-hand smoke (figure legends add cigarettes per day). Total nicotine equivalents 2.000 (95% CI 1.100–3.500) against 27.90 (23.80–32.70) nmol, about 93% lower (t = 8.53); NNAL 4.887 (3.817–6.257) against 203.5 (181.7–227.9) pg, about 98% lower (t = 27.96); acrolein marker 108.0 (95.93–121.6) against 271.5 (255.1–289.0) ng, 60% lower; acrylonitrile marker 3.959 (3.002–5.219) against 123.9 (109.9–139.7) ng, 97% lower; acrylamide marker 56.05 against 136.4 ng, 59% lower; naphthalene marker about 62% and pyrene marker 47% lower; cadmium 0.193 against 0.277 ng, 30% lower. Nearly all other metals and three volatile markers (toluene, benzene, carbon disulfide) were statistically similar. Overall lower in the vape-only group: all major nicotine metabolites, 2 minor alkaloids, all nitrosamines, 1 metal, all polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and 17 volatile compounds. Percentages recomputed by the editors from the printed means.

Against the 1,655 adults who had never used tobacco, the group that only vaped had higher levels of all major nicotine metabolites and total nicotine equivalents, all nitrosamines, 4 metals, 1 polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon and 4 volatile-compound markers (1,571 never-used against 220 vape-only people for the volatile-compound markers): NNAL 0.921 (0.819–1.035) in the never-used group against 4.887 (3.817–6.257) pg/mg (never-used group about 81% lower; t = 7.73); lead 0.351 against 0.432 and cadmium 0.149 against 0.193 ng/mg (19% and 23% lower); pyrene marker 0.128 against 0.161 ng/mg (20% lower); acrylonitrile marker 1.315 against 3.959 ng/mg (about 66% lower).

The 792 adults who both smoked and vaped had higher levels than the 2,411 who only smoked (769 against 2,322 for the volatile-compound markers), at similar numbers of cigarettes a day (15.1 against 15.4; t = 0.34): total nicotine equivalents 43.70 (39.80–48.10) against 27.90 (23.80–32.70) nmol/mg (the smoking-only group about 36% lower; t = 4.78); NNAL 262.6 (240.0–287.3) against 203.5 (181.7–227.9) pg/mg (23% lower); pyrene marker 15%, acrolein marker 10% and acrylonitrile marker 15% lower in the smoking-only group; lead (0.500 against 0.479) and cadmium (0.280 against 0.277 ng/mg) did not differ. Within the dual group, markers rose with how often people smoked (exploratory sub-group analyses; the authors say certain dual-use groups, for example some-days vaping with some-days smoking, may reflect the product last used).

Of the 247 adults who only vaped, 93% (229) had smoked cigarettes before (the former established smokers among them, who had smoked at least 100 cigarettes in their lifetime, had quit a mean of 3.5 years earlier and had smoked a mean of 19.0 cigarettes a day), only 18 had never smoked, 56% (147) vaped every day, and only 59% (161 people, percentage as printed) reported using nicotine-containing e-cigarettes (38% of the dual group); 44% used flavored ones. Cross-sectional analysis of Wave 1 only (Abstract). Authors' stated limits: device generation not recorded; cadmium in the group that only vaped may remain from earlier smoking (long half-life, 93% had smoked); most markers have short half-lives (mean 1.5 to 10 hours); the 2013–2014 period corresponds to the increasing availability of first-generation devices, and later-generation devices may give higher exposure, so the results may be conservative; e-cigarettes may also generate unique exposures (nickel and chromium given as examples) or exposures not designated as harmful constituents, such as those tied to flavorings; some volatile-compound laboratory results were outstanding when the analyses were run, so weighted estimates for those markers may not reflect the target population. Weighted response 54.0% for the household screener and 63.6% for the adult interview among those giving urine.

Nine studies (1,299 adults who smoked and were given e-cigarettes; follow-up one week to 8 months; Greece, Italy, Poland, UK, US). Pooled exhaled carbon monoxide, mean difference in ppm: vaping only against smoking only −9.57 (95% CI −17.30 to −1.83; 3 studies); vaping only against both −4.40 (−12.04 to 3.24; 2 studies); both against smoking only −1.91 (−3.38 to −0.45; 2 studies). Heterogeneity was substantial in every comparison, which the authors say reflects size and not direction; the figure legends note low baseline exhaled carbon monoxide in all groups of the study with 8-month values. Pooled values are those printed in the abstract (forest plots are images).

Other biomarkers came from five studies. Vaping only against smoking only (13 biomarkers): 12 lower with vaping, none higher, one (NNN) not different; Table 1 shows these rows rest on two studies, Cravo 2016 (n = 419 at baseline; its biomarker data come from a subset confined in week 1) and Morris 2022 (n = 79 at baseline; Table 1 uses its larger sample, study 1), both marked as tobacco or e-cigarette industry funded and rated high risk of bias. Vaping only against both (25 biomarkers): 12 lower with vaping only, 5 lower with both (all polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon metabolites, from one study of 22 people; statistical significance unclear), 8 not different or inconsistent. Both against smoking only (one study, Morris 2022; 13 biomarkers): 12 lower with both, NNN not different. In McRobbie 2015 a mercapturic acid marker fell in both the vape-only and dual groups over 4 weeks with no between-group difference.

Only one study had abstainers (Kerr 2020, a University of Glasgow document that appears to be a thesis): exhaled carbon monoxide at 12 weeks was 1 ppm (SD 1) both in the vaping group (n = 16) and in abstainers (n = 12), and abstainers were 18.00 ppm lower than the cigarette group (n = 3; 95% CI −24.81 to −11.19). Blood carboxyhaemoglobin (percentage saturation) at day 14 (n = 14, as printed) in study 1 of the Morris 2022 confinement study (days 1 to 9 vaping for all, then randomised to vaping, cigarettes or both for days 10 to 14), least-squares mean differences: vaping against cigarettes −7.13 (−8.41 to −5.85); vaping against both −2.56 (−3.81 to −1.31); both against cigarettes −4.57 (−5.90 to −3.25).
Results › Carbon monoxide, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Table 1 footnote; Endnote (study 1 and study 2)

Overall risk of bias was high in 8 of 9 studies and low in 1 (Cobb 2021, 520 people); two studies are marked industry funded (Cravo 2016, n = 419; Morris 2022, n = 79); devices were cig-a-likes, refillable, pods, cartridges or unclear. Authors' stated limits: data came from short confinement studies that do not generalise readily or from non-randomised groupings open to unmeasured confounding; for every outcome other than carbon monoxide there were too few data to pool; products varied; no individual participant data; only one study gave data on abstainers. Scope: nicotine exposure was not analysed (the authors say it is not necessarily a measure of harm).

Conclusions 5-1 to 5-3 (the committee's judgments): most e-cigarette products contain and emit numerous potentially toxic substances besides nicotine (5-1, conclusive); the number and amount vary widely with product and how the device is operated (5-2, conclusive); except for nicotine, under typical conditions of use, exposure to potentially toxic substances is significantly lower than from combustible tobacco cigarettes (5-3, substantial). Chapter 18 sets out four direct comparisons of smoke and aerosol: levels of selected toxicants in smoke 9 to 450 times those in aerosol (calculated from published data assuming 15 puffs per cigarette); toxicants emitted 82 to more than 99% lower per puff, depending on the regulatory list and puffing method (150 chemicals examined, 25 detected); about 1,500 times more harmful or potentially harmful constituents in smoke than in aerosol or room air; of 11 metals, higher in the aerosol for four, within the smoke range for five and lower for two.

Conclusion 18-1 (the committee's judgment: conclusive evidence): completely substituting e-cigarettes for cigarettes reduces exposure to numerous toxicants and carcinogens in cigarette smoke. The chapter's synthesis says all studies showed significantly reduced biomarkers of exposure in people who substituted e-cigarettes for cigarettes. Examples: a 5-day randomized study of 105 people (urinary biomarkers 29 to 95% lower and exhaled carbon monoxide 27 to 89% lower after partial or complete switching; people who used both products and replaced half their cigarettes had 7 to 38% reductions and 1 to 20% higher nicotine equivalents); 40 people followed for four weeks (exhaled carbon monoxide 80% lower with e-cigarettes only and 52% lower with both products; acrolein metabolite 3-HPMA 79% and 60% lower); and a cross-sectional comparison of 181 people in five groups in which long-term exclusive e-cigarette use had lower NNAL than every other group while nitrosamine and volatile-compound metabolites in people who used both products were similar to those in people who only smoked. Studies ranged from 13 to 420 people with follow-up of 5 days to 12 weeks, apart from one randomized study of 48 people followed for 8 months; the 12-week trial of a manufacturer's product (developed by Fontem Ventures B.V., per Chapter 18) had 40.2% compliance in its unconfined phase.

Tobacco-specific nitrosamines were found in e-liquids and aerosol at low levels, typically similar to those in pharmaceutical nicotine products (the chapter says this is probably attributed to pharmaceutical-grade nicotine); one study of 12 brands found two nitrosamines in aerosol from all but three, and another of three liquids found none in 100-puff aerosol. Carbonyls such as formaldehyde, acetaldehyde and acrolein in aerosol were in most cases lower than in smoke (for example 86 to 544 times lower for three carbonyls in one comparison), but very high formaldehyde levels were also reported. Metals: aerosol contains metals (5-4, substantial), whose origin could be the coil, other device parts or the liquid; the number of metals could be greater than in cigarette smoke except cadmium, which is markedly lower (5-5, limited); few, mostly small studies of first- and second-generation devices; one biomarker study of 64 people supported an inhaled contribution to the internal dose of chromium and nickel.

Chapter 7, other toxicants: nine studies (1 from the UK, no meta-analyses): the very limited findings generally suggested levels lower in people who vape than in people who smoke and higher than in people who use no nicotine. Carbon monoxide (33 studies, 3 from the UK): two meta-analyses against people who smoke both found significantly lower blood carboxyhaemoglobin; none against people who use no nicotine, but interventional studies suggested that exposure in people who switch completely might fall to levels like those of people who use no nicotine. Metals (10 cross-sectional studies, none from the UK, no meta-analyses): relative findings mixed; absolute findings mixed, most showing higher exposure in people who vape. Secondhand exposure (6 studies): short exposures gave no detectable change in nicotine, volatile compound or nitrosamine biomarkers; longer exposures during heavy sustained vaping gave significant increases.

The authors' reading (Chapter 7, Implications): compared with smoking, vaping leads to a substantial reduction in biomarkers of toxicant exposure, but the degree of any residual risk remains unclear, mainly because of a lack of comparisons between long-term former smokers who do and do not vape, or with people who have never smoked or vaped. Most studies had some methodological concerns; a lack of difference from people who use no nicotine may reflect insensitive methods, background exposures or truly similar exposure. Historical tobacco use can greatly affect many biomarkers and most people who vape previously smoked for a long time; the authors ask for strict definitions of exclusive vaping and biological checks of status. They state that many pooled findings came from tobacco industry-funded randomized trials in confinement lasting up to 7 days and call for independent research outside confinement and with longer follow-up.

evidence_set: PATH Waves 1 to 5: 24,027 adults analysed (50% under age 35, 51% women). Incident self-reported heart disease or stroke: 1,487 (764 of 14,832 who currently used neither product (the nonuse group, which includes former smokers); 41 of 822 who only vaped; 569 of 6,515 who only smoked; 113 of 1,858 who did both); heart attack, heart failure or stroke: 519 (222; 15; 242; 40). Age-adjusted rates per 1,000 person-years as printed: 8.0, 9.7, 14.8, 17.1 for any disease; 2.5, 4.0, 6.9, 7.1 for the narrower outcome (not reproducible from the counts: editors' check). Multivariable hazard ratios against nonuse, any disease: only vaping 1.00 (95% CI 0.69–1.45), only smoking 1.53 (1.30–1.79), both 1.54 (1.21–1.96); heart attack, heart failure or stroke: 1.35 (0.75–2.42), 2.20 (1.73–2.81), 2.08 (1.40–3.09). Adjusted for age, sex and race/ethnicity only: only vaping 1.16 (0.82–1.66) and 1.55 (0.87–2.76).

Multivariable hazard ratios against people who only smoked: only vaping 0.66 (0.46–0.94) for any disease and 0.61 (0.34–1.09) for heart attack, heart failure or stroke; both 1.01 (0.81–1.26) and 0.94 (0.65–1.36). The authors conclude that combining smoking with e-cigarette use does not reduce cardiovascular events and that quitting both is required to mitigate risk; no separate group that quit both was analysed, the group that only vaped did not differ detectably from nonuse (no current use of either product; includes former smokers), and the interval for both against smoking only (0.81–1.26) includes a 19% lower rate.
Table 1, columns 'Compared with Exclusive Smoking' and 'Compared with Nonuse'; Text, 7th and last paragraphs

Exposure and outcome: smoking = more than 100 lifetime cigarettes and current smoking; e-cigarette use = any current use, categories updated at each wave; outcome = self-reported past-12-month diagnosis (Waves 2 to 5) of heart attack or bypass surgery, heart failure, other heart condition or stroke; follow-up at most four years. Excluded before analysis: 5,873 lost at Wave 2, 2,172 previously diagnosed with cardiovascular disease, 55 missing exposure, 99 with baseline disease, 94 missing Wave 2 outcome data (of 32,320). People who only vaped or did both were younger (62% and 54% under 35 against 51%) and had more pack-years (mean 11.0 and 15.7 against 4.2 in the reference group, which includes people who had stopped smoking). Authors' stated limits: self-reported non-adjudicated outcomes that could be misclassified; short follow-up for a slowly developing disease; a reference group that includes people who had stopped smoking; few events in people who used e-cigarettes. Editors' note: the printed ± values for pack-years (46.7, 32.2, 21.8; the source does not name them, presumably standard deviations) are about 4, 2 and 5 times the means.

PATH Waves 1 to 4: 21,618 adults with no respiratory condition at baseline (14,213 never, 5,076 former, 2,329 current e-cigarette use); 1,460 (6.8%) had at least one new diagnosis (asthma 804, emphysema 336, COPD 573, chronic bronchitis 948). Multivariable-adjusted incidence rate ratios against never use for any respiratory condition: ever 1.28 (95% CI 1.10–1.48), former 1.28 (1.09–1.51), current 1.31 (1.08–1.59). Adjusted rates per 1,000 person-years: never 20.41 (18.65–22.17), ever 26.06 (22.63–29.49), former 26.12, current 26.68 (21.83–31.52). By condition (ever / former / current; analysed samples chronic bronchitis 25,202, emphysema 23,686, COPD 23,236, asthma 20,914): chronic bronchitis 1.33 / 1.31 / 1.33; emphysema 1.54 / 1.42 / 1.69; COPD 1.62 / 1.66 / 1.57; asthma 1.24 (1.01–1.53) / 1.19 (0.95–1.50) / 1.32 (1.01–1.72). Adjusted rates per 1,000 person-years, never against ever: COPD 6.48 against 10.49; emphysema 3.74 against 5.76; bronchitis 12.18 against 16.23; asthma 10.73 against 13.31.

Exposure was recorded at the first wave only; former use means ever use, even 1 or 2 puffs, and not now; current use means every day or some days; retention 83.2% (Wave 2), 78.4% (Wave 3), 73.5% (Wave 4). Outcomes were self-reported diagnoses from a physician or other health professional in the past 12 months. Authors' stated limits: self-reported exposure and diagnoses; observational data with relatively short follow-up, so causality could not be established; no time-varying exposure or confounding; a few important device characteristics (for example generation and flavor) not available or incomplete in the first wave; changes in lung-function tests may not appear until years after exposure (the authors call for serial tests). They also describe reverse causation (people with early symptoms switching to e-cigarettes or quitting) as a bias that could hide an association.

Conclusion 9-1 (the committee's judgment: no available evidence): whether e-cigarette use is associated with clinical cardiovascular outcomes (coronary heart disease, stroke, peripheral artery disease) or subclinical atherosclerosis; the chapter says there are no epidemiological studies of these outcomes. Conclusion 9-2 (substantial): heart rate rises shortly after nicotine intake; 9-3 (moderate): diastolic blood pressure rises; 9-4 (limited): short-term rise in systolic blood pressure, changes in biomarkers of oxidative stress, increased endothelial dysfunction and arterial stiffness, and autonomic control; 9-5 (insufficient): long-term changes in heart rate, blood pressure and cardiac geometry and function. Behind them: 13 short-term clinical studies (2010 to 2017; mostly crossover; healthy adults aged 23 to 39 on average) and three longer studies (34 people cross-sectional; a cessation trial (183 people with complete follow-up; 145 in its cohort analysis); a record-based cohort of 89 hypertensive patients); none measured clinical or subclinical atherosclerosis outcomes.

Conclusion 11-1 (the committee's judgment: no available evidence): whether e-cigarettes cause respiratory disease in humans. 11-2 and 11-3 (limited): better lung function and symptoms in adults who smoke and have asthma, and fewer COPD exacerbations in adults who smoke and have COPD, after switching completely or partly, from small retrospectively selected studies, mostly from one region of Italy, with the one randomized trial (12 weeks) finding no lung-function difference between people who switched and people who kept smoking. 11-4 (moderate): more cough and wheeze in adolescents who use e-cigarettes and an association with more asthma exacerbations, from four cross-sectional self-reported studies; 11-5 (limited): adverse respiratory effects in animal and cell studies. The chapter says studies of long-term effects on chronic respiratory symptoms are completely lacking.

Conclusion 10-1 (no available evidence): whether e-cigarette use is associated with intermediate cancer endpoints in humans, compared with smoking or with no tobacco use; the chapter calls the literature devoid of rigorous epidemiology on intermediate endpoints, let alone cancer. The only two human studies that refer to cancer: a 24-month cohort in which 'any cancer' was reported under serious adverse events (2 of 97 vaping only, 3 of 363 smoking only, 0 of 37 both; the committee's calculated risk ratio 2.49, 95% CI 0.42 to 14.72, for vaping only with smoking only as the referent; the data are called extremely limited by sample size and quality) and a 65-person study of mouth cells (more micronuclei in people who used e-cigarettes than in people who neither smoked nor used them, but the e-cigarette group was on average 10 years older). 10-2 (limited): in vivo animal studies using intermediate biomarkers support the hypothesis that long-term use could increase cancer risk, with no adequate long-term animal bioassays; 10-3 (limited): aerosol can be mutagenic or cause DNA damage in humans, animal models and human cells in culture; 10-4 (substantial): formaldehyde and acrolein can cause DNA damage, which supports the biological plausibility that long-term exposure could increase cancer risk; whether exposure levels are high enough to contribute to human carcinogenesis remains to be determined.

Chapter 11 (cardiovascular): as in 2018, to date there is still no available evidence on whether vaping is associated with clinical cardiovascular outcomes (coronary heart disease, stroke, peripheral arterial disease) or subclinical atherosclerosis. Overall, the extent to which vaping presents a risk for cardiovascular health remains uncertain, though the authors expect the risk to be much less than that of cigarette smoking based on the toxicant profile. 27 of the 41 included studies were cross-over or acute-exposure designs, which can address immediate effects but cannot answer questions about the cardiovascular health outcomes most relevant to public health; the authors call for studies comparing rates of coronary heart disease, peripheral arterial disease and stroke between people who use no nicotine, people who use tobacco and people who vape. No study was found in people with an existing cardiovascular condition. Animal studies (16) suggest possible long-term changes; no human evidence.

Chapter 9 (cancer): the National Academies found no available evidence on whether the chemicals in vaping aerosols or vaping behaviour were associated with cancer risk relative to smoking or non-use, and the Committee on Toxicity found existing evidence insufficient; this review calls the human literature growing but still modest. Biomarkers of exposure to several carcinogens are lower in people who vape than in people who smoke (the authors call this conclusive evidence of lower exposure); inflammation and oxidative stress findings show no systematic relationship and are insufficient to draw conclusions; gene expression and DNA methylation studies (8, none from the UK) are constrained by methodological limitations (for example, a lack of smoking comparison groups in some studies); no study assessed people with an existing or previous cancer; cell and animal studies are hard to translate. The authors state that biomarker studies need longer follow-up to show whether vaping reduces cancer risk compared with smoking. No cancer incidence data are presented.

Scope and cut-off (Chapters 2, 7, 11 and 16): the authors conducted two systematic reviews (health risks of vaping; harm perceptions); for the health chapters they first summarised previous reports by Public Health England, the National Academies and the Committee on Toxicity, then their own review, using an algorithm to decide on meta-analyses (Table 6 of Chapter 2 of the full report, not seen). Their two review protocol questions concern (1) the effect of vaping and secondhand exposure on markers associated with the risk of health conditions and (2) the effects of vaping among people with existing health conditions on disease outcomes; for cardiovascular disease and for exposure markers no study addressed the second. The search cut-off for the health chapters was July 2021, and the authors note that new studies have since been published and recommend continual updating. Databases, search terms, screening and risk-of-bias tool are not named on the pages read.
